questions.q: Match each behaviour to the bias behind it.
pairs: Refusing to sell a fallen share until it's back to what you paid
Buying because everyone online is buying
Assuming last year's big rise will continue
Trading often because you're sure you can beat the market
questions.why: Naming the bias is the first step to building a rule against it.

questions.q: According to Kahneman and Tversky's research, roughly how strongly does a loss feel compared with an equal gain?
questions.why: Losses feel roughly twice as painful as equal gains feel good, which pushes people to sell in panics and hold losers too long.

questions.q: You've already put £2,000 into a share that's now worth £1,200. What's the best question to ask?
options: If I had £1,200 in cash today, would I buy this share?
How do I get my £2,000 back?
What did I pay for it?
questions.why: The £800 lost is a sunk cost. Decide from here, as if starting fresh.

questions.q: Funds earned {f} a year, but investors in them earned {i} a year because of when they bought and sold. What's the behaviour gap, in percentage points?
questions.why: {f} − {i} = {answer} percentage points a year, lost to timing decisions, not to the funds themselves.

questions.q: A share that's doubled because lots of people are buying it is likely to be a sound investment.
questions.why: Popularity and a rising price aren't evidence of value. That's herding, and late buyers in bubbles often lose most.

questions.q: Checking your investments every day usually helps you make better decisions.
questions.why: Daily checks show many small losses, which feel worse than gains feel good, and tempt you to act on noise.

questions.q: A crash hits. Put these steps in the order a calm investor might follow.
items: Wait before acting: no trades today
Check your timeframe and goals haven't changed
Keep the monthly direct debit going
questions.why: Pause, consult the plan written while calm, check nothing real has changed, and stay the course.

questions.q: Match each bias to a guardrail that helps.
pairs: Keep a decision journal and review it honestly
Wait 48 hours before buying anything trending
Set your mix from goals, not recent returns
questions.why: Systems beat willpower: each rule blocks a specific bias.

questions.q: "This share used to be £10, so at £4 it must be a bargain." Which bias is this mainly?
questions.why: The old price is an anchor. What matters is the company's value now, not where the price once was.

questions.q: Explain why automating your investing (a monthly direct debit into a fund) helps against behavioural biases.

ideas.label: It removes the need to decide each time, so emotions don't make the decision
You keep buying through falls instead of panicking or trying to time the market

questions.model: Once it's automatic, you don't have to decide each month, so fear, greed and hype don't get a vote. You keep buying through falls (often at lower prices) instead of panicking or trying to time the market.

tests.answer: It happens automatically so emotions don't decide, and you keep buying through a crash instead of panicking.
You don't have to think about it.
Because direct debits pay more interest.

questions.q: Explain how loss aversion can lead investors to sell at exactly the wrong time.

ideas.label: Losses feel much worse than gains, so falling prices cause panic
They sell after a fall, locking in the loss and missing the recovery

questions.model: Because losses feel about twice as painful as gains, a falling market causes panic. Investors sell to stop the pain, usually after prices have already fallen, which locks in the loss and means missing the recovery.
questions.why: The urge to stop the pain sells at the low.

tests.answer: Losses hurt more than gains so people panic and sell after a fall, locking in the loss and missing the recovery.
They want to buy more shares.
